rv.q: After two hours of tuneful entertainment my carapace of skepticism had been breached, leaving warm appreciation oozing out.
Though some of its ingredients are fluffy or icky it eventually whisks up a satisfying mixture of whimsy, warmth, and sadness.
“A romcom set in the workplace and a feminist drama in which the protagonist makes painful progress to the belatedly assertive moment when she boots out her smugly abusive husband.

It's like someone's taken a tried-and-trusted Delia Smith recipe and created a gourmet version. Every ingredient is the best quality – the songs, the direction, the choreography, and the characters each combined in a careful, complementary way.
Waitress has bags of charm and polish – but also a little too much sugar.
There's really a lot to like; I just struggled to like all of it all at once.
If only everything about the show were as imaginative as its central notion.
I had a congenial enough time, but it's one of those productions where you can feel the plot grinding towards the next eruption of whoops from the stalls.
All in all, Waitress is a treat.

Ultimately Waitress is a simple story, but this production is anything but plain. It has all the quality ingredients required to serve up a delicious, perfectly baked show, sprinkled with wholesome life lessons and a dash of unexpected spice.
As the lead, Katherine McPhee brings to the role something special. I'd go as far and say that her 'She used to be mine' is the best I've heard in any musical production.
Diane Paulus directs it all with a deft touch and perfect pace; pitching the comedy just right but slowing things down for the more heart-wrenching moments.
Perhaps this musical plays on the expected, but it doesn't make it any less delightful.
Yet it's one of a series of only fleeting highlights in a production, directed by Diane Paulus, that flatlines elsewhere.
Waitress is not to all tastes. Despite efforts at realism showing life's sour side, the show is (sorry) too sweet.

cn.t: Critics find Waitress a charming, bittersweet confection elevated by Sara Bareilles' excellent score and strong performances, though some fault its overly sweet, lightweight approach to darker themes.
